title: Argentina’s October money growth came from term deposits and renewed commercial lending
bank: Banco Central de la República Argentina
summary: Argentina’s central bank reports that private-sector peso money balances grew in October even as the balances most readily used for payments fell. The difference lies in the composition of deposits. In real, seasonally adjusted terms private transactional M2 declined 0.4% during October, while fixed-term deposits rose 1.1% and private M3 increased 0.8%. The monthly change in transactional balances also looks different from the recent trend, because their average monthly change over the three months to October was slightly positive. The November publication describes developments during October. The report provides monetary and banking observations, without announcing a policy-rate decision (executive summary and section 2).

Cash held by the public grew 0.8% in real, seasonally adjusted terms, while transactional demand deposits fell 1.3%. Term deposits grew for a third consecutive month. Most of the increase in October came from corporate depositors outside the financial-services-provider category. Deposits held by individuals were broadly steady, while holdings by financial services providers declined alongside the assets of money market funds. The wholesale term-deposit rate, TAMAR, closed October at 24.1%, compared with 20.2% on individual deposits. Both changed little over the month. Broad private money reached 13.1% of GDP, 2.1 percentage points above its April 2024 low. These details qualify any reading of the headline as a widespread move by households into interest-bearing accounts (charts 2.1–2.2).

The creation of central bank money had several offsetting parts. Net purchases of foreign currency from the private sector amounted to USD 1.396 billion and added peso liquidity. Some was absorbed through Treasury operations, including auctions that raised more than the value of maturing debt and left the proceeds at the central bank. Open-market and repo operations also sterilized excess liquidity. Chart 3.1.1 reconciles the nominal change between month-end balances, while chart 3.1.2 describes changes in average real, seasonally adjusted balances. On the latter basis, the monetary base grew 1.1% in October and by an average of 1.7% per month over the latest three months (section 3.1).

Banks’ peso lending to the private sector rose 0.5% in real, seasonally adjusted terms. Commercial credit increased 0.9% after two months of contraction, with gains in both lending against commercial paper and advances. Secured loans grew 2.7%, including a 3.8% increase in mortgages. Housing purchase loans were up 28.6% in real terms over twelve months, primarily on the strength of loans indexed to the UVA unit. Consumer lending fell 0.6%. Card financing declined 1.2% while personal loans rose 0.1% after eight consecutive decreases. Combining both currencies, private credit grew 0.4% during the month. Peso loans represented roughly 9% of GDP and the stock of credit in both currencies reached 12.3% (section 3.2 and charts 3.2.1–3.2.4).

Foreign-currency deposits and loans moved differently. Private foreign-currency deposits rose USD 915 million to USD 42.883 billion, while the foreign-currency loan stock held around USD 26.350 billion. At the central bank, international reserves ended October at USD 48.565 billion, up USD 2.474 billion. Foreign-currency purchases and higher reserve-account balances contributed positively. Payments to international financial institutions and valuation changes worked in the other direction. The change in gross reserves thus gives a different number from the central bank’s net currency purchases. For someone assessing demand for pesos or the resilience of bank funding, those distinctions between currency, holder and balance-sheet entry matter as much as the aggregate growth rates (section 4 and the indicator tables in section 6).

questions.question: Will the concentration of term-deposit growth among companies persist?
questions.detail: The latest figures show corporate placements growing while individual holdings remain broadly stable. A temporary shift in companies’ cash management could reverse more quickly than a broad change in demand for term deposits. Compare deposit stocks by holder, interest rate and maturity over subsequent months, alongside money market fund assets and transactional accounts. This would show whether aggregate private M3 growth has become more diversified.

questions.question: How much of the peso liquidity created by foreign-currency purchases will remain in circulation?
questions.detail: Treasury balances, repos and open-market operations offset part of the October injection. Foreign-exchange purchases alone therefore give an incomplete picture of reserve money. Reconcile subsequent daily balance-sheet flows, Treasury auction settlements and changes in banks’ holdings with the real monthly-average base. Separate movements at month-end from persistent shifts so that differing reference dates do not drive the conclusion.

questions.question: Does the recovery in commercial and secured credit signal a broader change in borrower demand?
questions.detail: One month of renewed commercial lending and persistent mortgage growth coexist with a further fall in credit-card financing. The outstanding stocks combine new originations, repayments and, for indexed products, balance adjustments. Compare new lending volumes, maturities and repayment performance across loan types, with an explicit adjustment for UVA indexation. That evidence would help distinguish a durable credit expansion from movements confined to particular portfolios.
